data.title: The smith of Vršatec – iron tools from the time of Great Moravia
data.excerpt: Beneath the Vršatec crags in the White Carpathians a bulldozer struck a hoard of iron tools left behind by a Slavic smith at the end of the 9th century. Metallographic analysis of his axe, short scythe and unfinished currency bar shows that he already knew how to weld harder, carbon-rich iron onto a cutting edge – and the destroyed foundations of his smithy leave open the question of why no one ever came back to it.
data.metaTitle: The smith of Vršatec – tools from the time of Great Moravia
data.metaDescription: Beneath the Vršatec crags a hoard of iron tools from a 9th-century Slavic smithy came to light, alongside Lusatian and Púchov culture occupation.

children.text: Vršatecké Podhradie (Oroszlánko 1348, Podhrady 1470) lies in the White Carpathians at the foot of the Vršatec crags. Since 1970 the Vršatec rock formation has been a protected natural formation on account of its calcicolous flora. A settlement and a cremation cemetery of the Lusatian culture of the Late Bronze Age, a settlement of the Púchov culture from around the turn of the era, Slavic occupation of the 9th century and a hoard of iron tools belonging to a 9th-century Slavic smith were found here.
Hear an ancient tale, hidden from the books of men
A tale that lives to this day in the twilight of the forest
In the twilight of vanished paths, in the breath of woodland halls
Written in the bark of the oaks that faithfully shade them
Demons whisper it in the lap of the new moon
It is mirrored in the eyes of hidden limpid pools
Slavic occupation of Vršatec

That Vršatec was occupied by the Slavs in the Early Middle Ages was already pointed out by Petrovský-Šichman, who identified a continuous area of Slavic settlement in the gully of a brook that flows from the northern side beneath the castle. The extent of the settlement, as was later established, was far greater than the one hectare Šichman assumed, and the Slavs occupied both sides of the lower part of the valley. Part of their settlement lies on a gentle slope directly beneath the castle crags. Perhaps these castle crags too were occupied and fortified already in the Slavic period. A two-part quernstone was found at the north-western edge of the settlement. In addition, a large amount of typical Slavic pottery with wavy-line decoration was found here.

children.text: Immediately below the lower part of the settlement a low rampart runs from one side of the little valley to the other, and a second, similar rampart lies at the highest point of the valley below the summit of Chmelová. Not even the excavation by the Slovak Academy of Sciences in the 1960s produced a convincing answer to the question of whether the ramparts protected the Slavic settlement or a Hallstatt settlement, traces of which were also discovered here. It is assumed that on the spot where the picturesque remains of the stone castle of Vršatec rise there was a hilltop hillfort in the period of Great Moravia, which may have served above all as a refuge for the inhabitants of the settlement that spread out below it. With an elevation of around 700 m it is one of the highest-lying settlements in the Váh region altogether.
The mysterious Great Moravian smith
By the Green Wood there lived a smith called Jasmuz
Old age had caught up with him, yet had taken none of his strength
White hair in a braid and wrinkles on his face
And in the ravines of those wrinkles the smith's wisdom was carved

During construction work on a holiday resort in mountain terrain in the 1960s, a bulldozer struck an archaeological find, a large quantity of Slavic smith's tools. A rescue excavation confirmed that the building work had completely destroyed the foundations of a production feature, probably a smithy of the late 9th to the early 10th century.

blocks.text:
Radiance gives way to shadow, radiance brings the new to life
Shadow gives way to radiance, shadow gives new form to the living
In the forests and within the walls of the smithy
The same law, the same mighty dream
The smith knows the oldest of cycles
When he draws a blade, a horseshoe, out of the fire
Flames in the forge, flames in the clouds
The hammer whirls up a glowing snow of sparks

children.text: The first find
of March 1965 consisted of three
anvils, a chisel, four pairs of smith's tongs, two axes, an obsta, a coulter, a small symmetrical ploughshare, a hoe, a grubbing hoe
and several pieces of iron – semi-finished material.
The second part
of the hoard was discovered in August 1965 at the same spot. It comprised
an axe, an obsta, a short scythe
and a partly worked
iron currency bar.

blocks.caption: The smith of Vršatec as imagined by Tomáš Humaj
blocks.alt: The smith of Vršatec as imagined by Tomáš Humaj

children.text: The whole assemblage of objects found forms an organic unit, so that we can entirely rule out the possibility that this is a store of iron objects intended as scrap for further working. It is therefore unambiguous that at Vršatecké Podhradie tools and finished products from an old smithy were discovered, and we can date this assemblage of finds to the end of the 9th or possibly the beginning of the 10th century.
Jasmuz never forgot what must be heeded
To bow to the powers that guard the order of the forest
To bow to the trees whose wood he burned in his fire
He gave thanks for the herbs and for the honey of wild bees

Seen more closely in the light of the political events of the time, the smithy from Vršatecké Podhradie is either the workshop of a Great Moravian smith who supplied his products to the surroundings of this peripheral area of Great Moravia, or of a smith who, after the raids of the Magyars or of internal enemies at the beginning of the 10th century, left the lower-lying, threatened territory of Great Moravia and moved into a sheltered mountain valley in order to continue making his products there.

blocks.caption: A reconstruction of a smithy by B. Klíma (Mikulčice)
blocks.alt: A reconstruction of a smithy by B. Klíma (Mikulčice)

children.text: A further question arises: whether we may assume a centre of iron production in the vicinity, or whether iron in the form of so-called axe-shaped currency bars (one of which also comes from our find) was imported from more distant areas, either from the Uničov region or from the Slovenské rudohorie (the Slovak Ore Mountains). It is known, however, that not far from Vršatecké Podhradie, on the northern slope of Mount Hašková, iron ore was mined in the modern period. Perhaps this deposit was already known in the time of Great Moravia or even earlier.
How did the smith make them?
Axes, knives, weapons
Such are the tools that glow in the forge
The red-hot iron is cut
Until the shapes ripen into brilliant treasures

Let us look in more detail at the way the Vršatec axe was made, which will serve to illustrate the technology of producing objects of this type in the time of Great Moravia. The axe is well preserved. Its elongated shape widens towards the cutting edge. The butt is rectangular. The length of the axe is 205 mm, the width of the cutting edge 65 mm. The method and sequence of its manufacture were as follows. The axe was forged from a flat strip which was bent into the shape of an eye at the point of the shaft-hole and, in the working part, forged together again with one further sheet of material in order to increase the thickness between the hole and the cutting edge. The widening of the cutting edge was achieved by forging out to the sides, so that the individual sheets become thinner towards the edge. The axe was forged from two materials with different carbon contents. The part with the higher percentage of carbon was, as the harder one, understandably used for the cutting edge of the axe. During working by forging the iron was heated to a high temperature and then cooled relatively quickly. No other method of heat treatment was observed.

blocks.alt: The inventory of the smith's workshop from Vršatec

children.text: The partly worked currency bar that was found is a sheet of forged iron tapering towards both ends; its length is 168 mm. An examination of micro-purity revealed impurities similar to those in the axe. The whole object is made from a single piece of iron, so that no differences in carbon content, as in the case of the axe, were established, and the structure is homogeneous.

The short scythe, 310 mm long, is of elongated shape with a rectangular cross-section. At the working end it is bluntly finished; the other end narrows slightly to the point where it bends and narrows sharply into a tang, which served for mounting the handle. The scythe is made of two different sheets of iron, each with a different carbon content. In cross-section it is visible that these are two materials forged flat together, where the upper layer is of almost pure iron, while the lower part has a ferritic-pearlitic structure. From these facts we conclude that already at the time this scythe was made the Vršatec smith was aware that iron with a higher carbon content has greater hardness. We have already been able to observe a similar phenomenon in the case of the axe. Sheets of iron with a higher carbon content were therefore placed on the cutting edges of tools. In this tool a relatively small quantity of impurities, which would form inclusions and oxides between the two layers of metal, was established.

The obsta is a U-shaped tool 165 mm long with parallel arms tapering conically into points onto which handles were driven. The whole tool was forged from a single piece of material. The test of micro-purity revealed a considerable quantity of impurities. The fineness of the structure indicates that the object was finish-forged at a low temperature.

blocks.text:
Praised throughout the whole land
Was the ironwork of that old man
Who, so grown together with the world of the forest,
Forged his heart to all the anvils of silence

children.text: We have thus established that the Slavic smith at Vršatecké Podhradie already knew the method of welding a harder (carbon-richer) part of iron onto the functional part of a tool (the axe, the short scythe). We have come to know the method of making an axe from several strips of raw material; we have established that before forging the product was heated to a high temperature; we have further established that some objects, especially small and thin ones, were finish-forged only at a low temperature (obstarávacej). We have also seen certain technological shortcomings, such as the quantity of impurities in the iron.

blocks.text:
One day – why was the silence undone?
Someone rode up, bearing himself proudly high
From up there he looked down on the man, on Jasmuz
His steed a beggar, with no shoe on its hind leg

Dull guards without feeling now serve the prince faithfully
And he, the madman, demands the same armour for all
Through all the wicked humiliation Jasmuz still keeps his face
Only a true king may give such orders to a smith

children.text: Why did he leave?

blocks.caption: The scythe and the partly worked currency bar
blocks.alt: The scythe and the partly worked currency bar

children.text: Who was that mysterious smith of Vršatec? Was he born directly beneath the picturesque Vršatec crags, or did he merely take refuge in the valley from the raging of the wild Magyar hordes in the south? Whom did he supply with his products? Was his smith's art known far around? And where did he learn it? Why did he not finish his last currency bar? What fate befell this important man and those close to him? How is it possible that after his death, or after he left the smithy, no one returned to it and continued the smith's craft? If Vršatec was taken by an enemy at that time, it is all the more incomprehensible why the victors did not take the smith's precious tools and products with them, but left them untouched where they lay? Was the hoard of iron objects found at the hillfort at Pružina, only a few kilometres from Vršatec, the work of our smith of Vršatec? Questions, questions, questions. The last of them could be answered by a metallographic analysis of the Pružina hoard. For most of them, however, we shall probably no longer find unambiguous answers. Or will you try?

blocks.alt: The smith of Vršatec from the time of Great Moravia

blocks.text:
Jasmuz sleeps now...
Jasmuz sleeps now...
The day seems to have darkened, and yet it shines
Röri lifts the wounded body
Beyond the rainbow bridge there is another world
Death settles in the old man's face
It was a treacherous guard in the prince's service
Who with a deadly blow dims the hopes of all
Then the smith whispers an apology through his tears
"Forgive me, Lady, that I disturbed your peace." Beneath an enchanted fir Jasmuz lies down to sleep, free, and sinks into a dream The forge has gone out like the light in Jasmuz's eyes Never again will it belch forth a swarm of glowing sparks The hammers no longer beat like the smith's ardent heart Never again will it make any enchanted armour The smithy has grown cold like the old man's arms Never again will the clang of tools resound in that room In the Green Wood grief has settled upon all Jasmuz has fallen asleep, he gave away his wealth... Jasmuz sleeps now... Jasmuz sleeps now...
